title: The Labor Market for Recent College Graduates
key_claim: Through the second quarter of 2026 the unemployment rate for recent US college graduates stayed elevated at about 5.6 percent and the underemployment rate edged up to 42 percent.
frame_summary: Presents recent-graduate labour outcomes as a continuing quarterly series without attributing the weakness to any single cause, so the numbers constrain rather than confirm any explanatory story.
verbatim_quote: Labor market conditions remained challenging for recent college graduates through the second quarter of 2026. The unemployment rate stayed elevated at about 5.6 percent, and the underemployment rate edged up to 42 percent.
notes: Evergreen quarterly data feature, updated February, May, August and November; cited on its 2026:Q2 vintage. Quote confirmed by hand against the live page during the 22/08/2026 WebFetch sweep.

title: Youth employment amidst cooling labour demand, ECB Economic Bulletin Issue 5/2026
key_claim: The ratio of the euro area youth unemployment rate to the total unemployment rate rose to 2.4 in Q1 2026 from 2.1 in Q1 2023, but youth employment developments are broadly in line with normal cyclical dynamics once GDP growth is accounted for.
frame_summary: Argues that weaker euro area youth employment is mostly cyclical normalisation once GDP growth is accounted for, and cautions against reading it as AI-driven displacement.
verbatim_quote: The ratio of the youth unemployment rate to the total unemployment rate rose to 2.4 in the first quarter of 2026 from 2.1 in the first quarter of 2023, underlining that the labour market situation of young workers has weakened in relative terms.
verbatim_list: When compared with GDP growth, recent developments in youth employment are broadly in line with normal cyclical dynamics.
notes: Tier 1 euro-area counterweight to the US-centred evidence, and the principal source for the cyclical counter-argument. Quote confirmed by hand against the live page during the 22/08/2026 WebFetch sweep.

title: No Widespread Displacement, but the AI Employment Gap for Young Workers Has Widened to 19%
key_claim: Employment among workers aged 22 to 25 in highly AI-exposed occupations sits about 19% below where it would be had it kept pace with less-exposed peers, with declines concentrated in codified-knowledge occupations and increases among experienced workers in tacit-knowledge occupations.
frame_summary: Argues that AI's labour-market effect so far is not aggregate displacement but a redistribution against codified-knowledge work, and insists explicitly that the patterns are descriptive rather than causal estimates of AI's effect.
verbatim_quote: Employment among workers ages 22–25 in highly AI-exposed occupations now stands about 19% below where it would be if it had kept pace with employment among similarly aged workers in less-exposed occupations. Experienced workers show no comparable gap.
verbatim_list: In levels, employment of workers ages 22–25 in the two most exposed quintiles fell about 11% between November 2022 and June 2026, while employment of the same age group in the three least-exposed quintiles grew about 10%.

Employment has declined among young workers in occupations that rely heavily on codified knowledge: formal, standardized, documented knowledge that can be taught through education, textbooks, or written procedures. In contrast, employment has increased among experienced workers in occupations that rely more heavily on tacit knowledge acquired through practice, mentorship, and repeated exposure to real situations.
The adjustment appears to operate primarily through reduced hiring of young workers rather than increased separations.
notes: Spine source. The August 2026 revision introduces the codified-versus-tacit mechanism this scan is built on. Authors explicitly disclaim causal identification; the scan mirrors that caution. Quote confirmed by hand against the live page during the 22/08/2026 WebFetch sweep.

title: Borrowed expertise: Why AI's productivity boom may not survive the generation that built it
date_evidence:
Niam Yaraghi Nonresident Senior Fellow - Governance Studies, Center for Technology Innovation (CTI)

July 10, 2026
key_claim: Current AI productivity gains rest on a stock of expertise built before AI, and firms cutting junior hiring are dismantling the mechanism by which they historically produced their own senior judgement.
frame_summary: Argues that today's AI productivity gains draw down a stock of expertise built before AI, and that by collapsing entry-level hiring firms are dismantling the mechanism by which they historically produced their own senior judgement; frames this as a coordination failure requiring collective or policy response.
verbatim_quote: The juniors a firm does not hire today are the seniors that firm will not have in 15 years.
verbatim_list: Seyed Mahdi Hosseini and Guy Lichtinger, analyzing resume and job-posting data covering 65 million workers across 280,000 firms, found that companies actively adopting generative AI sharply reduced junior hiring relative to non-adopting firms, while senior employment in the same firms remained mostly unchanged.

If every firm in an industry independently decides not to hire juniors, the entire industry's senior pipeline empties out together, and there is nowhere for any firm to recruit the senior expertise it will need, because the cohort that would have produced it was never trained.
notes: Second Tier 2 spine source, supplying the coordination-failure argument. Author is a nonresident senior fellow writing commentary rather than peer-reviewed research; treated as institutional analysis. Quote confirmed by hand against the live page during the 22/08/2026 WebFetch sweep.

title: Many recent grads say AI is making it harder to get a job. Economists aren't so sure
key_claim: Brynjolfsson attributes the young-worker gap to large language models being trained on codified knowledge, while Deming and Humlum argue remote work and firm-level hiring data point away from AI as the cause.
frame_summary: Frames the entry-level squeeze as a live disagreement among labour economists rather than a settled AI story, giving equal weight to the remote-work and firm-spending counter-explanations.
verbatim_quote: But AI models lack the wisdom that comes with on-the-job experience or tacit knowledge that isn't written down.
verbatim_list: Second, Brynjolfsson says, large language models are trained on codified knowledge — information that has been written down in a textbook or document.

"If you look very carefully at the timing, it looks like the decline in junior hiring actually started a bit like six months before ChatGPT was released. And so what that tells me is it's something else," Deming says. "I think it's more like remote work."
notes: Carries both the mechanism quote and the strongest published dissent. Quote confirmed by hand against the live page during the 22/08/2026 WebFetch sweep.

title: AI Layoffs Backfire as 32% of Bosses Rehire Roles They Thought Robots Could Do
key_claim: Robert Half found 32 per cent of nearly 2,000 US hiring managers scrapped a role primarily because of AI and then brought the work back; Ford rehired 350 veteran engineers and IBM found its HR assistant resolves 94 per cent of routine queries but not the remaining 6 per cent.
frame_summary: Argues that the rehiring wave shows AI substitution was misjudged and that the durable pattern is complementarity, pairing AI with experienced staff on judgement work, rather than a story about the training pipeline.
verbatim_quote: Across all industries, 32 per cent said they had scrapped a role primarily because of AI, only to bring the work back soon after. The survey covered nearly 2,000 US hiring managers.
verbatim_list: Its AskHR assistant resolves 94 per cent of routine human resources queries, but the remaining 6 per cent, including cases that call for ethical judgment, still need a person, the company said.

Ford has hired, promoted or rehired 350 veteran engineers over the past three years, a group it calls its 'gray beard' engineers, to mentor younger staff and fix quality problems that automated systems could not solve.
Workforce analytics firm Orgvue found that 39 per cent of business leaders made staff redundant specifically because of AI, and 55 per cent of them later admitted the decision was a mistake.
'If we don't continue to invest in entry-level hires, what happens in three to five years?' said IBM chief human resources officer Nickle LaMoreaux. 'There's no pipeline. The well simply dries up.'
notes: Underlying data are the Robert Half and Orgvue surveys, both vendor-produced; treated as reported-through-journalism and used directionally. Quote confirmed by hand against the live page during the 22/08/2026 WebFetch sweep.

title: Does AI eliminate jobs? Economists find heavy adopters hire more.
key_claim: Across more than 21,000 US firms, companies in the top third of AI spend intensity grew headcount 10.2% over the two years after adoption, with entry-level headcount growing 12%.
frame_summary: Argues from firm-level spending data that heavy AI adoption complements hiring rather than replacing it, with entry-level roles expanding fastest at the heaviest adopters, which cuts directly against a pipeline-contraction reading.
verbatim_quote: Entry-level headcount grew even faster. At the companies making the largest AI investments, entry-level headcount grew 12% over the two years following adoption.
notes: Tier 4 vendor research using Ramp card and bill-pay data joined to Revelio Labs workforce records. Used only as directional counter-evidence; the authors themselves flag selection into AI adoption. Quote confirmed by hand against the live page during the 22/08/2026 WebFetch sweep.
